scope: Physics AS photoelectric/matter-wave applications and taught Chemistry Born–Haber/Kp A2 and Period 3 AS, school-mock only
notes: Five newly authored AQA-style problems with five distinct datasets, not official AQA past-paper content. Formula methods and numbers need human marking review for legitimate equivalent alternatives.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: AQA mock specification application
questions.prompt: In a model photoelectric experiment, the stopping potential Vs is 0.50 V when light frequency is 6.00×10¹⁴ Hz and 1.74 V at 9.00×10¹⁴ Hz. Assume the graph of Vs (vertical axis) against f (horizontal axis) is straight. Use electron charge e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C. (a) Determine the graph gradient. (b) Deduce a value for Planck's constant h. (c) Find threshold frequency f₀ and work function φ in joules. (d) State the effect of doubling the light intensity at unchanged frequency above threshold on maximum kinetic energy and on the number of electrons emitted per second. [8 marks]
markPoints: From eVs=hf−φ the gradient of Vs against f is h/e.
Deduce h = e×gradient = (1.60×10⁻¹⁹)(4.13×10⁻¹⁵) = 6.61×10⁻³⁴ J s.
Set Vs=0 and extrapolate: f₀=6.00×10¹⁴−0.50/(4.133×10⁻¹⁵) ≈ 4.79×10¹⁴ Hz.
Work function φ = hf₀ ≈ 3.17×10⁻¹⁹ J.
In electronvolts the work function would be ≈ 1.98 eV, consistent with the above.
At a fixed frequency above threshold, doubling light intensity does not change maximum photoelectron kinetic energy.
The photoelectron emission rate increases because more photons arrive each second.
questions.modelAnswer: Graph gradient ΔVs/Δf = (1.74−0.50)/((9.00−6.00)×10¹⁴) = 4.13×10⁻¹⁵ V s. From eVs=hf−φ the gradient of Vs against f is h/e. Deduce h = e×gradient = (1.60×10⁻¹⁹)(4.13×10⁻¹⁵) = 6.61×10⁻³⁴ J s. Set Vs=0 and extrapolate: f₀=6.00×10¹⁴−0.50/(4.133×10⁻¹⁵) ≈ 4.79×10¹⁴ Hz. Work function φ = hf₀ ≈ 3.17×10⁻¹⁹ J. In electronvolts the work function would be ≈ 1.98 eV, consistent with the above. At a fixed frequency above threshold, doubling light intensity does not change maximum photoelectron kinetic energy. The photoelectron emission rate increases because more photons arrive each second.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: AQA mock specification application
questions.subtopic: Electron matter wavelength from accelerating voltage
questions.prompt: An electron initially at rest gains kinetic energy by travelling through a potential difference of 150 V. Use electron charge e = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C, electron mass m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg and Planck constant h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s. Ignore relativistic effects. (a) Calculate kinetic energy, electron momentum and de Broglie wavelength. (b) Predict the wavelength for 600 V and justify the scaling. (c) Explain why a measured electron diffraction pattern supports wave–particle duality. [7 marks]
markPoints: Electron kinetic energy Eₖ=eV=1.60×10⁻¹⁹×150=2.40×10⁻¹⁷ J.
Use non-relativistic Eₖ=p²/(2m), hence p=√(2mEₖ).
Momentum p≈6.61×10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹.
Apply the de Broglie equation λ=h/p.
Wavelength at 150 V is λ≈1.00×10⁻¹⁰ m.
Quadrupling acceleration voltage from 150 V to 600 V doubles momentum, so λ halves to ≈5.01×10⁻¹¹ m.
Diffraction patterns arise from wave interference, showing that electrons also have wave behaviour.

Apply the de Broglie equation λ=h/p. Wavelength at 150 V is λ≈1.00×10⁻¹⁰ m. Quadrupling acceleration voltage from 150 V to 600 V doubles momentum, so λ halves to ≈5.01×10⁻¹¹ m. Diffraction patterns arise from wave interference, showing that electrons also have wave behaviour.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: AQA mock specification application
questions.prompt: For an illustrative Born–Haber cycle of MgO(s), use these values (kJ mol⁻¹): standard enthalpy of formation ΔHf°(MgO) = −602; atomisation Mg(s) → Mg(g) +148; first and second Mg ionisation energies +738 and +1451; ½O₂(g) → O(g) +249; first and second electron affinities of O(g) −141 and +844. (a) Define lattice enthalpy of formation. (b) Calculate MgO lattice enthalpy of formation, showing each term and the sign. [8 marks]
markPoints: Lattice enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of solid ionic compound forms from its constituent gaseous ions.
Mg atomisation contributes +148 kJ mol⁻¹.
Mg first and second ionisation energies together contribute +738 +1451 = +2189 kJ mol⁻¹.
Converting half a mole of oxygen molecules to gaseous oxygen atoms contributes +249 kJ mol⁻¹.
Oxygen first electron affinity contributes −141 kJ mol⁻¹.
Oxygen second electron affinity contributes +844 kJ mol⁻¹.
Sum of the gaseous-ion formation steps = 148+738+1451+249−141+844 = +3289 kJ mol⁻¹.
By Hess's law −602 = +3289 + ΔHlattice formation, so ΔHlattice formation = −3891 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.modelAnswer: Lattice enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of solid ionic compound forms from its constituent gaseous ions. Mg atomisation contributes +148 kJ mol⁻¹. Mg first and second ionisation energies together contribute +738 +1451 = +2189 kJ mol⁻¹. Converting half a mole of oxygen molecules to gaseous oxygen atoms contributes +249 kJ mol⁻¹. Oxygen first electron affinity contributes −141 kJ mol⁻¹. Oxygen second electron affinity contributes +844 kJ mol⁻¹. Sum of the gaseous-ion formation steps = 148+738+1451+249−141+844 = +3289 kJ mol⁻¹. By Hess's law −602 = +3289 + ΔHlattice formation, so ΔHlattice formation = −3891 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: AQA mock specification application
questions.subtopic: Equilibrium mole fractions, partial pressures and pressure response
questions.prompt: For the hypothetical equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), an initially pure sample contains 0.80 mol N₂O₄. At equilibrium 0.20 mol N₂O₄ has dissociated and the total equilibrium pressure is 150 kPa. (a) Find the equilibrium amounts of each gas and the total amount of gas. (b) Calculate both partial pressures and Kp including units. (c) Predict the effect of raising total pressure at constant temperature on the equilibrium position and on Kp. [7 marks]
markPoints: Equilibrium amount N₂O₄ = 0.80−0.20 = 0.60 mol.
From 1:2 stoichiometry the amount of NO₂ formed is 0.40 mol.
Total equilibrium amount = 0.60+0.40 = 1.00 mol.
Partial pressure of N₂O₄ = (0.60/1.00)×150 = 90 kPa.
Partial pressure of NO₂ = (0.40/1.00)×150 = 60 kPa.
Kp = p(NO₂)²/p(N₂O₄) = 60²/90 = 40 kPa.
Higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer gaseous molecules (N₂O₄), but Kp stays unchanged at the same temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibrium amount N₂O₄ = 0.80−0.20 = 0.60 mol. From 1:2 stoichiometry the amount of NO₂ formed is 0.40 mol. Total equilibrium amount = 0.60+0.40 = 1.00 mol. Partial pressure of N₂O₄ = (0.60/1.00)×150 = 90 kPa. Partial pressure of NO₂ = (0.40/1.00)×150 = 60 kPa. Kp = p(NO₂)²/p(N₂O₄) = 60²/90 = 40 kPa. Higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer gaseous molecules (N₂O₄), but Kp stays unchanged at the same temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: AQA mock specification application
questions.subtopic: Unfamiliar Period 3 melting comparisons across structures
questions.prompt: A student is asked to compare the melting points of Period 3 elements Na, Al, Si, P, S and Cl. For these conditions phosphorus exists as P₄ and sulfur as S₈. Explain the qualitative changes in melting point across the set, specifically Na→Al, Al→Si, Si→P₄, P₄→S₈ and S₈→Cl₂. Refer to the appropriate structure or bonding in each comparison. [6 marks]
markPoints: Sodium and aluminium both have giant metallic lattices.
Aluminium melts above sodium because stronger metallic electrostatic attraction results from higher ionic charge density and more delocalised electrons.
Silicon has a giant covalent lattice of strong covalent bonds, giving a very high melting point above the metallic elements in this set.
Phosphorus consists of simple P₄ molecules, so the sharp fall from silicon is due to only intermolecular forces between molecules rather than a giant covalent network.
S₈ molecules are larger with more electrons than P₄, so stronger London dispersion forces give sulfur a higher melting point than phosphorus.
Cl₂ molecules are smaller than S₈ with fewer electrons and weaker London forces, so chlorine melts at a lower temperature than sulfur.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium and aluminium both have giant metallic lattices. Aluminium melts above sodium because stronger metallic electrostatic attraction results from higher ionic charge density and more delocalised electrons. Silicon has a giant covalent lattice of strong covalent bonds, giving a very high melting point above the metallic elements in this set. Phosphorus consists of simple P₄ molecules, so the sharp fall from silicon is due to only intermolecular forces between molecules rather than a giant covalent network. S₈ molecules are larger with more electrons than P₄, so stronger London dispersion forces give sulfur a higher melting point than phosphorus. Cl₂ molecules are smaller than S₈ with fewer electrons and weaker London forces, so chlorine melts at a lower temperature than sulfur.
